Controllability and Stabilizability of the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system with Maxwell’s lawThanks: ∗Department of Mathematics & Statistics, Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, Kanpur, UP- 208016, India; e-mail: sakilahamed777@gmail.comThanks: † Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai- 400076, India; e-mail: subratamajumdar634@gmail.comThanks: ∗Corresponding author: Sakil Ahamed

Sakil Ahamed∗, and Subrata Majumdar†
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper, we study the control properties of the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system with Maxwell’s law around a constant steady state (ρs,us,0),ρs>0,us>0(\rho_{s},u_{s},0),\rho_{s}>0,u_{s}>0 in the interval (0,2​π)(0,2\pi) with periodic boundary data. We explore the exact controllability of the coupled system by means of a localized interior control acting in any of the equations when time is large enough. We also study the boundary exact controllability of the linearized system using a single control force when the time is sufficiently large. In both cases, we prove the exact controllability of the system in the space L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi). We establish the exact controllability results by proving an observability inequality with the help of an Ingham-type inequality. Moreover, we prove that the system is exactly controllable at any time if the control acts everywhere in the domain in any of the equations. Next, we prove the small time lack of controllability of the concerned system.

Further, using a Gramian-based approach demonstrated by Urquiza, we prove the exponential stabilizability of the corresponding closed-loop system with an arbitrary prescribed decay rate using boundary feedback control law.

Key words and phrases: 
Linearized compressible Navier-Stokes equation with Maxwell’s law, Exact controllability, Boundary control, distributed control, Ingham inequality, Observability inequality, Feedback stabilization

1. Introduction and Main results

1.1. Setting of the problem

The control and stabilization of fluid flow have been extensively studied due to their numerous practical applications such as weather prediction, water flow in a pipe, designing aircraft and cars. Many researchers have been interested in the subject of the controllability of fluid flows, more so for incompressible flow (see [2], [20], [35], [36], [39]) than for compressible flow (see [13], [14]). In our research, we focus on investigating the exact controllability and stabilizability of the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system with Maxwell’s law.

Let us consider the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system in the domain (0,2​π)(0,2\pi):

(1.1) ∂tρ^+∂x(ρ^​u^)=0 in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂t(ρ^​u^)+∂x(ρ^​u^2)+∂xp=∂xS^in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),}\left.\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\hat{\rho}+\partial_{x}(\hat{\rho}\hat{u})=0\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{ in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}\left({\hat{\rho}\hat{u}}\right)+\partial_{x}\left({\hat{\rho}\hat{u}^{2}}\right)+\partial_{x}p=\partial_{x}\hat{S}\qquad\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\end{aligned}\right\}

where, ρ^\hat{\rho}, u^\hat{u}, pp and S^\hat{S} represent the density, velocity, pressure and stress tensor of the fluid, respectively. Equation (1.1)1 is the consequence of conservation of mass and equation (1.1)2 is the consequence of conservation of momentum. We assume that the pressure pp satisfies the following constitutive law:

(1.2) p⁡(ρ^)=a​ρ^γ,γ≥1,p(\hat{\rho})=a\hat{\rho}^{\gamma},\>\quad\gamma\geq 1,

where aa is a positive constant. While, the stress tensor S^\hat{S} is assumed to satisfy the Maxwell’s law:

(1.3) κ​∂tS^+S^=μ​∂xu^, in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π).\kappa\partial_{t}\hat{S}+\hat{S}=\mu\partial_{x}\hat{u},\text{ in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi).

Here μ\mu and κ\kappa are positive constants, with μ\mu representing the fluid viscosity and κ\kappa denoting the relaxation time that characterizes the time delay in the response of the stress tensor to the velocity gradient. For more detailed information, refer to [23] and references therein. Relation (1.3) is first proposed by Maxwell, in order to describe the relation of stress tensor and velocity gradient for a non-simple fluid.

In this paper, we study the control aspects of the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes system with Maxwell’s law and with periodic boundary conditions linearized around a constant steady state (ρs,us,0),ρs>0,us>0\left(\rho_{s},u_{s},0\right),\rho_{s}>0,u_{s}>0 of (1.1). More precisely we consider the following system:

(1.4) ∂tρ+us∂xρ+ρs∂xu=𝟙𝒪1f1,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂tu+us∂xu+aγρsγ−2∂xρ−1ρs∂xS=𝟙𝒪2f2,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂tS+1κS−μκ∂xu=𝟙𝒪3f3,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),ρ(t,0)=ρ(t,2π),u(t,0)=u(t,2π),S(t,0)=S(t,2π),t∈(0,T),ρ(0,x)=ρ0(x),u(0,x)=u0(x),S(0,x)=S0(x),x∈(0,2​π),}\left.\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho+u_{s}\partial_{x}\rho+\rho_{s}\partial_{x}u=\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{O}_{1}}f_{1},\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}u+u_{s}\partial_{x}u+a\gamma{\rho_{s}}^{\gamma-2}\partial_{x}\rho-\frac{1}{\rho_{s}}\partial_{x}S=\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{O}_{2}}f_{2},\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}S+\frac{1}{\kappa}S-\frac{\mu}{\kappa}\partial_{x}u=\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{O}_{3}}f_{3},\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\rho(t,0)=\rho(t,2\pi),\>u(t,0)=u(t,2\pi),\>S(t,0)=S(t,2\pi),\qquad&&t\in(0,T),\\ &\rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad S(0,x)=S_{0}(x),\qquad&&x\in(0,2\pi),\end{aligned}\right\}

where 𝟙𝒪𝕛\mathbbm{1_{\mathcal{O}_{j}}} is the characteristic function of an open set 𝒪j⊂(0,2​π),{\mathcal{O}}_{j}\subset(0,2\pi), j=1,2,3j=1,2,3 and fif_{i}, i=1,2,3i=1,2,3 are the distributed controls.

Definition 1.1.

The system (1.4) is exactly controllable in (L2​(0,2​π))3(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3} at time T>0T>0, if for any initial condition (ρ0,u0,S0)⊤∈(L2​(0,2​π))3(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})^{\top}\in(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3} and any other (ρ1,u1,S1)⊤∈(L2​(0,2​π))3(\rho_{1},u_{1},S_{1})^{\top}\in(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3}, there exist controls fi∈L2(0,T;L2(𝒪i)),i=1,2,3,f_{i}\in L^{2}\left(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{i})\right),i=1,2,3, such that the corresponding solution (ρ,u,S)⊤(\rho,u,S)^{\top} of (1.4) satisfies

(1.5) (ρ,u,S)⊤​(T,x)=(ρ1,u1,S1)⊤​(x), for all ​x∈(0,2​π).(\rho,u,S)^{\top}(T,x)=(\rho_{1},u_{1},S_{1})^{\top}(x),\text{ for all }x\in(0,2\pi).

Let us first mention controllability results for some fluid models related to our system. The existence of the solution of the compressible Navier-Stokes system with Maxwell’s law, along with the blow-up results has been studied, for example, in [22, 23, 43] and references therein. If κ=0\kappa=0, then the Maxwell’s law (1.3) turns into the Newtonian law S^=μ​∂xu^\hat{S}=\mu\partial_{x}\hat{u} and the equation (1.1) becomes Navier-Stokes system of a viscous, compressible, isothermal barotropic fluid (density is function of pressure only), in a bounded domain (0,2​π)(0,2\pi). The compressible Navier-Stokes system linearized around a constant trajectory (ρs,us)(\rho_{s},u_{s}) for ρs>0,us>0\rho_{s}>0,u_{s}>0, yields a coupled transport-parabolic system with constant coefficients. The controllability of such systems with constant coefficients in one dimension has been extensively studied in the literature. In [10, 11], the authors studied this system in the domain (0,2​π)(0,2\pi) with periodic boundary conditions and localized interior control acting only in the parabolic equation. In [10], using the moment method, the authors proved the null controllability in Hms+1​(0,2​π)×Hs​(0,2​π),H^{s+1}_{\textnormal{m}}(0,2\pi)\times H^{s}(0,2\pi), s>6.5,s>6.5, at time T>2​π|us|,T>\frac{2\pi}{|u_{s}|}, where Hms​(0,2​π)H^{s}_{\textnormal{m}}(0,2\pi) is the space of periodic Sobolev space with mean zero. This result was improved in [11] by showing that the null controllability holds for any initial data in Hm1​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π).H^{1}_{\textnormal{m}}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi). Moreover, the authors also proved that, the system in consideration is not null controllable in Hms​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π),H^{s}_{\textnormal{m}}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi), 0⩽s<1,0\leqslant s<1, at any time T>0T>0 by L2L^{2}-control acting in the parabolic equation. Thus Hm1​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)H^{1}_{\textnormal{m}}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi) is the largest space in which the system is null controllable by a L2L^{2}-parabolic control.

Recently, in [3], the above results have been extended to more general coupled transport-parabolic systems with constant coefficients. The authors considered coupling of several transport and parabolic equations in one-dimensional torus 𝕋\mathbb{T} and studied the null controllability with localized interior control in optimal time. Moreover, an algebraic necessary and sufficient condition on the coupling term was obtained when controls act only on the parabolic or transport components. For the extension of these results to the general coupling matrix, one can refer to the work [25].

The local null controllability of the nonlinear compressible Navier-Stokes system around a trajectory with non-zero velocity at large time T>0T>0 has been obtained in [17, 16, 18, 33, 32, 34].

In [1], the authors considered the one-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations with Maxwell’s law linearized around a constant steady state (ρs,0,0),ρs>0(\rho_{s},0,0),\rho_{s}>0 with Dirichlet boundary conditions and with interior controls in the interval (0,π)(0,\pi). They have proved that the system is not null controllable at any time using localized controls in density and stress equations and even everywhere control in the velocity equation. Moreover, they have shown that the system is null controllable at any time T>0T>0 in the space (L2​(0,π))3(L^{2}(0,\pi))^{3}, if the control acts everywhere in the density or stress equation. Approximate controllability at large time using localized controls has also been studied.

In the following subsection, we state our main results regarding the interior controllability of the system (1.4)

1.2. Interior controllability

At first, we consider the case when f2=0=f3f_{2}=0=f_{3} in (1.4). Performing integration by parts and using the boundary conditions, from the system (1.4), we deduce

dd​t​(∫02​πu⁡(t,x)​𝑑x)=0,dd​t​(∫02​πS⁡(t,x)​etκ​𝑑x)=0,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\int_{0}^{2\pi}u(t,x)\>{\rm d}x\right)=0,\quad\frac{d}{dt}\left(\int_{0}^{2\pi}S(t,x)e^{\frac{t}{\kappa}}\>{\rm d}x\right)=0,

and therefore,

∫02​πu⁡(T,x)​𝑑x=∫02​πu0​(x)​𝑑x,∫02​πS⁡(T,x)​eTκ​𝑑x=∫02​πS0​(x)​𝑑x.\int_{0}^{2\pi}u(T,x)\>{\rm d}x=\int_{0}^{2\pi}u_{0}(x)\>{\rm d}x,\quad\int_{0}^{2\pi}S(T,x)e^{\frac{T}{\kappa}}\>{\rm d}x=\int_{0}^{2\pi}S_{0}(x)\>{\rm d}x.

Thus if the system (1.4) with f2=0=f3f_{2}=0=f_{3} is exactly controllable at time T>0T>0 then necessarily

(1.6) ∫02​πu0​(x)​𝑑x=0=∫02​πS0​(x)​𝑑x.\int_{0}^{2\pi}u_{0}(x)\>{\rm d}x=0=\int_{0}^{2\pi}S_{0}(x)\>{\rm d}x.

Since we’re working with a system governed by periodic boundary conditions, it is convenient to consider the Sobolev spaces for the periodic functions. For s∈ℕ∪{0}s\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, we denote by Hps​(0,2​π)H^{s}_{\text{p}}\left(0,2\pi\right), the space of 2​π2\pi-periodic functions belonging to Hlocs​(ℝ)H^{s}_{\text{loc}}\left(\mathbb{R}\right), and by H˙ps​(0,2​π)\dot{H}^{s}_{\text{p}}\left(0,2\pi\right), the subspace of the functions belonging to Hps​(0,2​π)H^{s}_{\text{p}}\left(0,2\pi\right), with mean value zero. Consequently, the space L˙2​(0,2​π)\dot{L}^{2}\left(0,2\pi\right), is given by

L˙2(0,2π)={f∈Lloc2(ℝ):f(x+2π)=f(x), for a.e. x∈ℝ,∫02​πf(x)dx=0}.\dot{L}^{2}\left(0,2\pi\right)=\left\{f\in L^{2}_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R}):\>f(x+2\pi)=f(x),\text{ for a.e. }x\in\mathbb{R},\>\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\,{\rm d}x=0\right\}.
Theorem 1.2.

Let f2=0=f3f_{2}=0=f_{3} in (1.4) and 𝒪1⊆(0,2​π)\mathcal{O}_{1}\subseteq(0,2\pi). Then there exists a T0>0T_{0}>0 such that the system (1.4) is exactly controllable in L2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times{\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)} at time T>T0T>T_{0}, by an interior control f1∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪1))f_{1}\in L^{2}\left(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{1})\right) for the density.

Remark 1.3.

In fact, if the control is used in one of the equations, then the following exact controllability results can be obtained:

  1. (1)

    Let f1=0=f3f_{1}=0=f_{3} in (1.4) and 𝒪2⊆(0,2​π)\mathcal{O}_{2}\subseteq(0,2\pi). Then the system (1.4) is exactly controllable in L˙2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π){\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)} at time T>T0T>T_{0}, by an interior control f2∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪2))f_{2}\in L^{2}\left(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{2})\right) for the velocity.

  2. (2)

    Let f1=0=f2f_{1}=0=f_{2} in (1.4) and 𝒪3⊆(0,2​π)\mathcal{O}_{3}\subseteq(0,2\pi). Then the system (1.4) is exactly controllable in L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π){\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)}\times L^{2}(0,2\pi) at time T>T0T>T_{0}, by an interior control f3∈L2​(0,T,L2​(𝒪3))f_{3}\in L^{2}\left(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O}_{3})\right) for the stress.

Remark 1.4.

Note that the characteristics equations associated to our system (1.4) can be written as:

x+β1​t=c1,x+β2​t=c2,x+β3​t=c3,x+\beta_{1}t=c_{1},\quad x+\beta_{2}t=c_{2},\quad x+\beta_{3}t=c_{3},

where c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3} are constants and β1,β2,β3\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3} are the roots (distinct and nonzero) of the equation

(1.7) r3+2​us​r2+(us2−b​ρs−μκ​ρs)​r−μ​usκ​ρs=0.r^{3}+2u_{s}r^{2}+\left(u_{s}^{2}-b\rho_{s}-\frac{\mu}{\kappa\rho_{s}}\right)r-\frac{\mu u_{s}}{\kappa\rho_{s}}=0.

In the above theorem, the waiting time T0T_{0} is of the form

T0=2​π​(1|β1|+1|β2|+1|β3|).T_{0}={2\pi}{\left(\frac{1}{|\beta_{1}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{2}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{3}|}\right)}.

In Theorem 1.2, the exact controllability result is proved for any time T>T0T>T_{0}. We can not claim that T0T_{0} is the minimal time to have the exact controllability of the system. Determine the minimal time Tm​i​n>0T_{min}>0, such that the system is exactly controllable at T≥Tm​i​nT\geq T_{min} and the system is not exactly controllable at T<Tm​i​nT<T_{min} is a challenging open problem. In particular, notice that the minimal control time should depend on the support of the localized control.

Next result regarding the controllability of the system when control acts everywhere in the domain.

Theorem 1.5.

Let f2=0=f3f_{2}=0=f_{3} in (1.4). Then for any T>0T>0 the system (1.4) is exactly controllable in L2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times{\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)} at time T>0T>0, by a control f1∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,2​π))f_{1}\in L^{2}\left(0,T;L^{2}(0,2\pi)\right) acting everywhere in the density.

Remark 1.6.

Additionally, we achieve exact controllability of the system (1.4) at time T>0T>0 by means of interior control acting either velocity or stress equation applied everywhere in the domain.

Next, let us study the controllability properties of the linearized compressible Navier–Stokes system with Maxwell’s law when the control acts only in the boundary.

1.3. Boundary controllability

Let us consider the following system:

(1.8) ∂tρ+us∂xρ+ρs∂xu=0,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂tu+us∂xu+aγρsγ−2∂xρ−1ρs∂xS=0,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂tS+1κS−μκ∂xu=0,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),ρ(0,x)=ρ0(x),u(0,x)=u0(x),S(0,x)=S0(x),x∈(0,2​π),}\left.\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho+u_{s}\partial_{x}\rho+\rho_{s}\partial_{x}u=0,\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}u+u_{s}\partial_{x}u+a\gamma{\rho_{s}}^{\gamma-2}\partial_{x}\rho-\frac{1}{\rho_{s}}\partial_{x}S=0,\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}S+\frac{1}{\kappa}S-\frac{\mu}{\kappa}\partial_{x}u=0,\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad S(0,x)=S_{0}(x),\qquad&&x\in(0,2\pi),\end{aligned}\right\}

along with one of the following boundary conditions in the time interval (0,T):(0,T):

(1.9) Control in density: ρ(t,0)=ρ(t,2π)+q(t),u(t,0)=u(t,2π),S(t,0)=S(t,2π),\displaystyle\textit{Control in density: }\rho(t,0)=\rho(t,2\pi)+q(t),\>u(t,0)=u(t,2\pi),\>S(t,0)=S(t,2\pi),
(1.10) Control in velocity: ρ(t,0)=ρ(t,2π),u(t,0)=u(t,2π)+r(t),S(t,0)=S(t,2π),\displaystyle\textit{Control in velocity: }\rho(t,0)=\rho(t,2\pi),\>u(t,0)=u(t,2\pi)+r(t),\>S(t,0)=S(t,2\pi),
(1.11) Control in stress: ρ(t,0)=ρ(t,2π),u(t,0)=u(t,2π),S(t,0)=S(t,2π)+p(t),\displaystyle\textit{Control in stress: }\rho(t,0)=\rho(t,2\pi),\>u(t,0)=u(t,2\pi),\>S(t,0)=S(t,2\pi)+p(t),

where q,r,pq,r,p, are the controls. We recall the definition of boundary exact controllability of the system (1.8)-(1.9).

Definition 1.7.

The system (1.8)-(1.9) is boundary exactly controllable in (L2​(0,2​π))3(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3} at time T>0T>0, if for any initial condition (ρ0,u0,S0)⊤∈(L2​(0,2​π))3(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})^{\top}\in(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3} and any other (ρ1,u1,S1)⊤∈(L2​(0,2​π))3(\rho_{1},u_{1},S_{1})^{\top}\in(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3}, there exists control q∈L2​(0,T)q\in L^{2}\left(0,T\right) such that the corresponding solution (ρ,u,S)⊤(\rho,u,S)^{\top} of (1.8)-(1.9) satisfies

(ρ,u,S)⊤​(T,x)=(ρ1,u1,S1)⊤​(x), for all ​x∈(0,2​π).(\rho,u,S)^{\top}(T,x)=(\rho_{1},u_{1},S_{1})^{\top}(x),\text{ for all }x\in(0,2\pi).

We now mention some boundary controllability results of the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system. In [10], the authors studied null controllability of the concerned system in Hms+1​(0,2​π)×Hs​(0,2​π),H^{s+1}_{\textnormal{m}}(0,2\pi)\times H^{s}(0,2\pi), s>4.5,s>4.5, using boundary control acting at the parabolic component at time T>2​π|us|T>\frac{2\pi}{|u_{s}|} with periodic boundary data. Recently, in the work [28], the above result has been improved. The author established the boundary null controllability of the system in the space L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi) using density control and in the space Hm1​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)H^{1}_{m}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi) using velocity control in time T>2​π|us|T>\frac{2\pi}{|u_{s}|}. This paper extends these two results for the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes equation with non-barotropic fluids. In the context of Dirichlet boundary, the paper [5] dealt with the boundary null controllability of this system with a density control in the space Hs​(0,1)×L2​(0,1),s>12H^{s}(0,1)\times L^{2}(0,1),s>\frac{1}{2} at time T>1T>1. The authors have also explored the approximate controllability of the system in the space L2​(0,1)×L2​(0,1)L^{2}(0,1)\times L^{2}(0,1) at time T>1T>1. Null controllability “up to a finite-dimensional space” in the space Hs​(0,1)×L2​(0,1),s>12H^{s}(0,1)\times L^{2}(0,1),s>\frac{1}{2} has been shown by a velocity control in time T>1T>1 with periodic boundary condition for density and Dirichlet boundary conditions for velocity.

1.4. Methodology of the proof of main results

The proof of the exact controllability result relies on an observability inequality and the spectral analysis of the linearized operator. The spectrum of the linear operator consists of three sequences of complex eigenvalues whose real parts converge to three distinct finite numbers, and the imaginary parts behave as nn for |n|→∞|n|\rightarrow\infty (see, Section 2.1). Therefore the system behaves like a hyperbolic system. Hence the geometric control condition is needed for the controllability of the system using localized control. Moreover, the eigenfunctions of the linearized operator and its adjoint form Riesz bases on L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi). Then using the series representation of the solution of the adjoint problem and a hyperbolic type Ingham inequality, we can prove Theorem 1.2. The proof of the Ingham-type inequality relies on the construction of a family biorthogonal to the family of exponentials {e−λkl​t,k∈ℤ∗,l=1,2,3}\{e^{-{\lambda_{k}^{l}}t},k\in\mathbb{Z}^{*},l=1,2,3\}, see Section 7. The technique we have adapted is inspired from [30] and [6]. The entire study relies on the theory of logarithmic integral and complex analysis. One can refer to the book [44] for more details. Moreover, it is worthwhile to mention that a modification (for example [11, Proposition 3.1] or [1, Proposition 8.1]) to the general hyperbolic Ingham inequality (see [24], [31, Theorem 4.1]) is not enough to prove the required Ingham-type inequality for our case.

The controllability result (Theorem 1.5) is established using a direct approach: constructing the control explicitly to bring the system’s solution at rest at any given finite time TT. Since the eigenfunctions (or the generalized eigenfunctions) of the linearized operator form a Riesz Basis, the system (1.4) with control acting everywhere in the domain can be projected onto each finite dimensional eigenspaces for each n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. For any given time T>0T>0, we can achieve null controllability of this finite-dimensional system using the ‘Hautus lemma’. Furthermore, constructing the control using the finite-dimensional controllability operator can be achieved alongside a uniform estimate that is independent of nn (see Lemma 3.6). Next, summing up these finite dimensional controls obtained for each projected system, we construct a control for the whole system and we show that the control brings the solution of the whole system to rest at time T>0T>0. This approach closely resembles that utilized in [12].

This paper also deals with the lack of controllability of the system (1.4). For the influence of the transport component of the system, it is relevant to guess that the system (1.4) cannot be steered to zero (as exact and null controllability are equivalent for our system) at small time (see Theorem 5.1). More precisely, in Section 5, we have established that, the system is not exactly controllable at small time by means of localized interior control acting on every equations. We have utilized the work [3, Section 3] to establish this result. Furthermore, we also proved that the control system (1.8), (1.10) is not controllable in small time with the boundary control acting in density. Similarly, the same result can be demonstrated for other boundary cases ((1.9), (1.11)) also.

1.5. Stabilizability

In this paper, we also study the boundary feedback stabilization of linearized compressible Navier-Stokes system with Maxwell’s law (1.8) with the control acting only in the any boundary of density (1.9), velocity (1.10) and stress (1.11). More precisely, we construct a feedback control law which forces the solution of (1.8)-(1.9) to decay exponentially towards the origin with any order.

In our case, we prove the exponential stabilization result by an explicit feedback law following a method demonstrated by J.M. Urquiza [38] which relies on the Gramian approach and the Riccati equations, see [40], [26] for more details. This method addresses the exponential stabilization issue for an exactly controllable system with an operator that generates an infinitesimal group of continuous operator. This approach has been successfully utilized to study rapid exponential stabilization of KdV equation [8], Boussinesq system of KdV-KdV type in [7], linearized compressible Navier-Stokes equation in the case of creeping flow in [9]. Our work regarding exponential stabilization is inspired from [8], [7] and [9]. Recently, classical moment method has been extensively utilized to establish the exact controllability and stabilizability of some dispersive system, see [41], [42]. In these works, utilizing the group structure of the corresponding system, the authors conclude the stabilizability from the controllability in some periodic Sobolev spaces.

Let us state the main stabilization result for the closed-loop system (1.8)-(1.9).

Theorem 1.10.

The control system (1.8)-(1.9) is completely stabilizable in L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi) by boundary feedback control q∈L2​(0,∞)q\in L^{2}\left(0,\infty\right) for the density. That is, for any ν>0\nu>0, there exists a continuous linear map Π:L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)×L2​(0,2​π)→ℂ\Pi:L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi)\times L^{2}(0,2\pi)\to\mathbb{C} such that for any initial data (ρ0,u0,S0)∈L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})\in\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi), the solution (ρ,u,S)(\rho,u,S) of system (1.8)-(1.9) with q⁡(t)=Π⁡((,,,,,))q(t)=\Pi(\left(\rho(t,\cdot),u(t,\cdot),S(t,\cdot)\right)) satisfies the following

‖ρ⁡(t,⋅)‖L2​(0,2​π)+‖u⁡(t,⋅)‖L2​(0,2​π)+‖S⁡(t,⋅)‖L2​(0,2​π)\displaystyle\left\|\rho(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L^{2}(0,2\pi)}+\left\|u(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L^{2}(0,2\pi)}+\left\|S(t,\cdot)\right\|_{L^{2}(0,2\pi)} ⩽C​e−ν​t​[‖ρ0‖L2​(0,2​π)+‖u0‖L2​(0,2​π)+‖S0‖L2​(0,2​π)],\displaystyle\leqslant Ce^{-\nu t}\bigg[\left\|\rho_{0}\right\|_{L^{2}(0,2\pi)}+\left\|u_{0}\right\|_{L^{2}(0,2\pi)}+\left\|S_{0}\right\|_{L^{2}(0,2\pi)}\bigg],

for all t>0t>0, where C=C⁡(T)C=C(T) is a positive constant, independent of ρ0,u0,S0,q\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0},q and tt.

1.6. Organization of the paper

The plan of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we investigate the well-posedness of the system (1.4) using semigroup theory and determine the adjoint of the linear operator associated with the coupled system. Next, in Section 2.1, we analyze the behavior of the spectrum of the linearized operator associated with system (1.4), demonstrating that the eigenfunctions of the linear operator form a Riesz basis in (L2​(0,2​π))3(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3}. The exact controllability results, Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.5, are proved in Section 3. The proof of the boundary exact controllability result, Theorem 1.8, is given in Section 4. In Section 5, we discuss the lack of controllability of system (1.4) in small time. Subsequently, in Section 6, we examine the rapid exponential stabilization result (Theorem 1.10). In Section 7, we present the proof of an Ingham-type inequality adapted to our context. Finally, in Section 8, we provide some details on managing multiple eigenvalues of the linear operator.

Proposition 2.3.

The adjoint of (𝒜,𝒟⁡(𝒜,𝒵))(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{{Z}})) in 𝒵\mathcal{{Z}} is defined by

and

Remark 2.7.

From the asymptotic behaviors (2.10)-(2.12) of the eigenvalues, it is clear that all eigenvalues are simple at least for large nn. Thus if there exist multiple eigenvalues depending on the system parameters ρs,us,b,κ,μ\rho_{s},u_{s},b,\kappa,\mu, they are finite in numbers.

For the case of multiple eigenvalues, the following results can be derived by appropriately introducing generalized eigenfunctions (for more details, see Section 8). From the previous remark, we observe that multiple eigenvalues of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, if they occur at all, are only finitely many. Since our later analysis requires the asymptotic behaviors of the coefficients of the eigenvectors, we will avoid the details of the explicit computation of the generalized eigenfunctions. However, for clarity, we will compute the generalized eigenfunctions of 𝒜\mathcal{A} in the case of double eigenvalues.

Thus, now onwards, we assume the following :

3. Interior controllability

This section is devoted to the exact controllability of the system (1.4) by means of localized interior control acting in any of the equations. Our proof relies on the duality between the controllability of the system and the observability of the corresponding adjoint system. Here we only prove the exact controllability result when the control acts only in the density equation. For the other two cases, the proofs follow in a similar fashion.

We recall the final state observability of (𝒜∗,ℬ∗):(\mathcal{A}^{*},\mathcal{B}^{*}): For (𝒜∗,𝒟⁡(𝒜∗,𝒵m))(\mathcal{A}^{*},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*};\mathcal{{Z}}_{m})) defined in (2.5)-(2.6) and (σT,vT,S~T)⊤∈𝒵m,(\sigma_{T},v_{T},\tilde{S}_{T})^{\top}\in\mathcal{{Z}}_{m}, we set

where 𝕋∗\mathbb{T}^{*} is the C0C^{0}-semigroup generated by (𝒜∗,𝒟⁡(𝒜∗,𝒵m))(\mathcal{A}^{*},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*};\mathcal{{Z}}_{m})) on 𝒵m\mathcal{{Z}}_{m}. In view of Proposition 2.3, (σ,v,S~)⊤(\sigma,v,\tilde{S})^{\top} belongs to C⁡([0,T],𝒵m)C([0,T];\mathcal{{Z}}_{m}) and satisfies:

Remark 3.3.

In the proof of Theorem 1.2, i.e, in the proof of the observability inequality (3.13), we assume that all the eigenvalues of 𝒜\mathcal{A} are simple to get the Ingham-type inequality for full class of exponentials {e−λnl¯​t:n∈ℤ∗,l∈{1,2,3}}.\{e^{-\overline{\lambda_{n}^{l}}t}:n\in\mathbb{Z}^{*},l\in\{1,2,3\}\}. In Remark 2.7, we have mentioned that the spectrum of 𝒜\mathcal{A} may have finite number of multiple eigenvalues. In this case also, one can prove the observability inequality with a slight modification of the technique for simple eigenvalue case. Details analysis can be found in [11, Section 4.2]. One can also refer to the book [27, Remarks, Page 178] for a version of Ingham inequality with repeated eigenvalues. In the next section, we discuss a brief description of the proof of concerned observability inequality.

3.1.1. The case of multiple eigenvalues

In this section, we prove null controllability of the system (1.4) with f2=f3=0f_{2}=f_{3}=0 in the presence of multiple eigenvalues. Our main goal is to prove the observability inequality (3.3). The proof will be similar for all cases (control acting in density or velocity or stress), so we present a detailed proof for the density case only. The proof is inspired from [27, Section 4.4] and [11, Section 4.2].

3.2. Control acting everywhere in the domain

Now, we proceed to prove Theorem 1.5. Since, exact and null controllability are equivalent for our system, we are going to prove the null controllability for the sake of computational simplicity. To do this, we first establish the null controllability of each finite-dimensional projected system (2.76), and then utilize this to infer the null controllability of the system (2.65).

Recall that (2.76) is defined on 𝐙n\mathbf{Z}_{n} with control from EnE_{n}, where 𝐙n\mathbf{Z}_{n} and EnE_{n} are finite-dimensional spaces defined in (2.61) and (2.70), respectively. Referring back to Lemma 2.12 and Lemma 2.13, the matrix representation of πn​𝒜|𝐙n\pi_{n}\mathcal{A}|_{\mathbf{Z}_{n}} and πn​ℬ|En\pi_{n}\mathcal{B}|_{E_{n}} is denoted as 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} and ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}, respectively. To assess the controllability of (2.76), we apply the “Hautus Lemma” (refer to [4, Theorem 2.5, Section 2, Chapter 1, Part I]) to the pair (𝒜n,ℬn)(\mathcal{A}_{n},\mathcal{B}_{n}).

3.2.1. Proof of Theorem 1.5 :

To establish Theorem 1.5, we aim to demonstrate that for any T>0T>0 and for any z0∈𝒵mz_{0}\in\mathcal{Z}_{m}, there exists a control f∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,2​π))f\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,2\pi)) such that the solution zz of (2.65) satisfies z⁡(T)=0z(T)=0 in 𝒵m\mathcal{Z}_{m}.

Additionally, the control fnf_{n} satisfies (3.35).

Now, let us set f=∑n∈ℤfnf=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{n}. Utilizing (3.35) and (2.58), we obtain f∈L2​(0,T,L2​(0,2​π))f\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(0,2\pi)) with:

where CC is a generic positive constant. With this control ff and the initial condition z0z_{0}, (2.65) admits a unique solution z∈C⁡([0,T],𝒵m)z\in C([0,T];\mathcal{Z}_{m}), which can be decomposed as z⁡(t)=∑n∈ℤzn​(t)z(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}z_{n}(t), where zn​(t)∈𝐙nz_{n}(t)\in\mathbf{Z}_{n} satisfies (2.76). 4. Boundary controllability

In this section, we will discuss the boundary controllability of the compressible Navier–Stokes system with Maxwell’s law (1.8) with any of the boundary conditions (1.9), (1.10) and (1.11). At first, we study the boundary controllability of the system (1.8), when the control acts only in density.

4.1. Control in density

Let us consider the system (1.8) with (1.9). For the reader’s convenience, we recall the system:

(4.1) ∂tρ+us∂xρ+ρs∂xu=0,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂tu+us∂xu+aγρsγ−2∂xρ−1ρs∂xS=0,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),∂tS+1κS−μκ∂xu=0,in ​(0,T)×(0,2​π),ρ(t,0)=ρ(t,2π)+q(t),u(t,0)=u(t,2π),S(t,0)=S(t,2π),t∈(0,T),ρ(0,x)=ρ0(x),u(0,x)=u0(x),S(0,x)=S0(x),x∈(0,2​π).}\left.\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho+u_{s}\partial_{x}\rho+\rho_{s}\partial_{x}u=0,\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}u+u_{s}\partial_{x}u+a\gamma{\rho_{s}}^{\gamma-2}\partial_{x}\rho-\frac{1}{\rho_{s}}\partial_{x}S=0,\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\partial_{t}S+\frac{1}{\kappa}S-\frac{\mu}{\kappa}\partial_{x}u=0,\qquad&&\text{in }(0,T)\times(0,2\pi),\\ &\rho(t,0)=\rho(t,2\pi)+q(t),\>u(t,0)=u(t,2\pi),\>S(t,0)=S(t,2\pi),\qquad&&t\in(0,T),\\ &\rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad S(0,x)=S_{0}(x),\qquad&&x\in(0,2\pi).\end{aligned}\right\}

4.1.1. Well-posedness

Like interior controllability cases, at first let us write the system (4.1) in the following abstract form:

(4.2) z˙​(t)=𝒜​z​(t)+ℬρ​q​(t),t∈(0,T),z⁡(0)=z0,\dot{z}(t)=\mathcal{A}z(t)+\mathcal{B}_{\rho}q(t),\quad t\in(0,T),\qquad z(0)=z_{0},

where we have set z⁡(t)=(ρ⁡(t,⋅),u⁡(t,⋅),S⁡(t,⋅))⊤,z(t)=(\rho(t,\cdot),u(t,\cdot),S(t,\cdot))^{\top}, z0=(ρ0,u0,S0)⊤z_{0}=(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})^{\top}. One can identify the operator 𝒜,ℬ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} through its adjoint by taking the scalar product of (4.2) with a vector of smooth functions (ϕ,ψ,ξ)(\phi,\psi,\xi) and comparing it with (4.1). 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the unbounded operator given by (2.2) with its domain

𝒟(𝒜;𝒵)={(ρuS)∈𝒵:(ρ,u,S)⊤∈H1(0,2π)×H1(0,2π)×H1(0,2π),ρ⁡(0)=ρ⁡(2​π),u⁡(0)=u⁡(2​π),S⁡(0)=S⁡(2​π).}.\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{Z})=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\rho\\ u\\ S\end{pmatrix}\in\mathcal{Z}\>:\>\left(\rho,u,S\right)^{\top}\in H^{1}(0,2\pi)\times H^{1}(0,2\pi)\times H^{1}(0,2\pi),\>\begin{aligned} &\rho(0)=\rho(2\pi),\\ &u(0)=u(2\pi),\\ &S(0)=S(2\pi).\end{aligned}\right\}.

The control operator ℬρ∈ℒ⁡(ℂ,𝒟​(𝒜∗)′)\mathcal{B}_{\rho}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C};\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})^{\prime}) defined by

⟨ℬρ​q​(t),(ϕ,ψ,ξ)⟩𝒟​(𝒜∗)′,𝒟⁡(𝒜∗)=q⁡(t)​(b​us​ϕ⁡(2​π)¯+b​ρs​ψ⁡(2​π)¯).\left<{\mathcal{B}_{\rho}q(t)},{(\phi,\psi,\xi)}\right>_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})^{\prime},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})}=q(t)\left(bu_{s}\overline{\phi(2\pi)}+b\rho_{s}\overline{\psi(2\pi)}\right).

Clearly ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{\rho} is well-defined as ℬρ​q\mathcal{B}_{\rho}q is continuous on H1​(0,2​π)×H1​(0,2​π)×H1​(0,2​π)H^{1}(0,2\pi)\times H^{1}(0,2\pi)\times H^{1}(0,2\pi) (by the embedding theorem H1​(0,2​π)↪C⁡[0,2​π]H^{1}(0,2\pi)\hookrightarrow C[0,2\pi]). Its adjoint ℬρ∗∈ℒ⁡(𝒟⁡(𝒜∗),ℂ)\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*});\mathbb{C}) is

(4.3) ℬρ∗(ϕ,ψ,ξ)=𝟙{x=2π}(b​usb​ρs0)(ϕ,ψ,ξ)=busϕ(2π)+bρsψ(2π).\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*}(\phi,\psi,\xi)=\mathbbm{1}_{\{x=2\pi\}}\begin{pmatrix}bu_{s}\\ b\rho_{s}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}(\phi,\psi,\xi)=bu_{s}{\phi(2\pi)}+b\rho_{s}{\psi(2\pi)}.

One can prove that the operator ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{{\rho}} satisfies the following so-called admissibility condition

(4.4) ∫0T|ℬρ∗​𝕋T−t∗​Φ|2​𝑑t⩽C​‖Φ‖𝒵,∀Φ∈𝒟⁡(𝒜∗),\int_{0}^{T}|\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*}\mathbb{T}_{T-t}^{*}\Phi|^{2}\,{\rm d}t\leqslant C\left\|\Phi\right\|_{{\mathcal{Z}}},\forall\,\Phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*}),

where CC is some positive constant. The proof relies on the explicit expression of the solution of the adjoint (3.1) and the right hand side inequality of (3.4). Indeed, performing an integration of the square of identity (4.17) over [0,T][0,T] and then applying (3.4), we get the required admissibility conditions.

Since 𝒜\mathcal{A} generates a contraction semigroup and ℬρ\mathcal{B}_{\rho} is an admissible operator, we can prove the following well-posedness result (see Theorem 2.372.37 in page 53 of [15], for more details):

Proposition 4.1.

Let T>0T>0, (ρ0,u0,S0)⊤∈L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})^{\top}\in\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi) and q∈L2​(0,T)q\in L^{2}(0,T). Then the system (4.1) has a unique solution (ρ,u,S)⊤∈C⁡([0,T],(L2​(0,2​π)3))(\rho,u,S)^{\top}\in C\left([0,T];(L^{2}(0,2\pi)^{3})\right) and the solution satisfies

‖(ρ,u,S)‖C⁡([0,T],𝒵)⩽C⁡(‖(ρ0,u0,S0)‖𝒵+‖q‖L2​(0,T)),\displaystyle\|(\rho,u,S)\|_{C([0,T];\mathcal{{Z}})}\leqslant C\Big(\|(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})\|_{\mathcal{{Z}}}+\|q\|_{L^{2}(0,T)}\Big),

where C=C⁡(T)C=C(T) is a positive constant, independent of ρ0,u0,S0,q\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0},q and tt.

4.1.2. Exact Controllability

In this section, we prove the exact controllability of the system (4.1). As interior control case, here at first we discuss the classical approach to deduce the observability inequality for the adjoint system (3.1) which essentially gives the exact controllability of the main system (4.1). Let us consider the linear map ℱT:L2​(0,T)→(L2​(0,2​π))3\mathcal{F}_{T}:L^{2}(0,T)\to(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3} by ℱT​(q)=(ρ⁡(T,⋅),u⁡(T,⋅),S⁡(T,⋅))⊤\mathcal{F}_{T}(q)=\left(\rho(T,\cdot),u(T,\cdot),S(T,\cdot)\right)^{\top}, where (ρ,u,S)(\rho,u,S) is the solution of the system (4.1) with (ρ0,u0,S0)=(0,0,0)(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})=(0,0,0). It is clear that exact controllability for (4.1) is equivalent to the surjectivity of the map ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}. Note that the map ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T} is surjective if and only if there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that the following inequality holds:

(4.5) ‖ℱT∗​𝐳‖L2​(0,T)≥C​‖𝐳‖(L2​(0,2​π))3, for all ​𝐳∈(L2​(0,2​π))3.\displaystyle\left\|\mathcal{F}_{T}^{*}\mathbf{z}\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T)}\geq C\left\|\mathbf{z}\right\|_{(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3}},\,\text{ for all }\mathbf{z}\in(L^{2}(0,2\pi))^{3}.

A direct computation shows that ℱT∗​((,,,,,))=b​us​σ​(t,2​π)+b​ρs​v​(t,2​π)\mathcal{F}_{T}^{*}((\sigma_{T},v_{T},\tilde{S}_{T}))=bu_{s}\sigma(t,2\pi)+b\rho_{s}v(t,2\pi), where (σ,v,S~)(\sigma,v,\tilde{S}) is the solution of the adjoint system (3.1) with the terminal data (σT,vT,S~T)(\sigma_{T},v_{T},\tilde{S}_{T}). Thus we get the following proposition.

Proposition 4.2.

The system (4.1) is exactly controllable in 𝒵m,m\mathcal{Z}_{m,m} at time T>0T>0 using a control qq in L2​(0,T)L^{2}(0,T) acting only in the density, if and only if, there exists a positive constant CT>0C_{T}>0 such that for any (σT,vT,S~T)∈𝒵m,m(\sigma_{T},v_{T},\tilde{S}_{T})\in\mathcal{Z}_{m,m}, (σ,v,S~)(\sigma,v,\tilde{S}), the solution of (3.1), satisfies the following observability inequality:

(4.6) ∫02​π|σT​(x)|2​𝑑x+∫02​π|vT​(x)|2​𝑑x+∫02​π|S~T​(x)|2​𝑑x⩽CT​∫0T|b​us​σ​(t,2​π)+b​ρs​v​(t,2​π)|2​𝑑t.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}|\sigma_{T}(x)|^{2}\,{\rm d}x+\int_{0}^{2\pi}|v_{T}(x)|^{2}\,{\rm d}x+\int_{0}^{2\pi}|\tilde{S}_{T}(x)|^{2}\,{\rm d}x\leqslant C_{T}\int_{0}^{T}|bu_{s}\sigma(t,2\pi)+b\rho_{s}v(t,2\pi)|^{2}\,{\rm d}t.

Before giving the proof of the above observability inequality, we mention the following lemma which ensures that the observation term is nonzero.

Lemma 4.3.

Let us recall the eigen functions ℰ(𝒜∗)={ξn,l∗| 1⩽l⩽3,n∈ℤ∗}\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{A}^{*})=\left\{\xi^{*}_{n,l}\>|\>1\leqslant l\leqslant 3,n\in\mathbb{Z}^{*}\right\} of the unbounded operator 𝒜∗.\mathcal{A}^{*}. Then we have the following result:

ℬρ∗​ξ≠0,∀ξ∈ℰ⁡(𝒜∗),\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*}\xi\neq 0,\forall\,\xi\in\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{A}^{*}),

where ℬρ∗\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*} is the observation operator associated to the system (4.1), defined by (4.3).

Proof.

Observe that, ℬρ∗​ξn,l∗=bψnl​(us​αn,l1+ρs​αn,l2).\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*}\xi^{*}_{n,l}=\frac{b}{{\psi}_{n}^{l}}\left({u_{s}\alpha^{1}_{n,l}+\rho_{s}\alpha^{2}_{n,l}}\right). From the first equation of the eigen equations 𝒜∗​ξn,l∗=λnl¯​ξn,l∗\mathcal{A}^{*}\xi^{*}_{n,l}=\overline{\lambda_{n}^{l}}\xi^{*}_{n,l}, we obtain

(4.7) bψnl​(us​αn,l1+ρs​αn,l2)=b​αn,l1​λnl¯ψnl​i​n=λnl¯ψnl​i​n≠0​( using (2.14),(2.45)).\frac{b}{{\psi}_{n}^{l}}\left({u_{s}\alpha^{1}_{n,l}+\rho_{s}\alpha^{2}_{n,l}}\right)=\frac{b\alpha_{n,l}^{1}\overline{\lambda_{n}^{l}}}{{\psi}_{n}^{l}in}=\frac{\overline{\lambda_{n}^{l}}}{{\psi}_{n}^{l}in}\neq 0\,(\text{ using }\eqref{negrealpart},\,\eqref{nmaxequ-psi_nl}).

Thus ℬρ∗​ξn,l∗≠0.\mathcal{B}_{\rho}^{*}\xi^{*}_{n,l}\neq 0. ∎

In a similar approach as density control case, we can also prove the exact controllability result (see Remark 1.9) of the system (1.8), when control acts only on the velocity or stress. In the following sections, we just indicate the changes according to the system (1.8) with (1.10) and (1.8) with (1.11).

Remark 4.4.

The proof of the observability inequality for the case of multiple eigenvalues can be demonstrated in a similar approach as done in the case of interior controllability in Section 3.1.1.

4.2. Control in velocity

Here the control operator ℬu∈ℒ⁡(ℂ,𝒟​(𝒜∗)′)\mathcal{B}_{u}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C};\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})^{\prime}) is defined by

⟨ℬu​r​(t),(ϕ,ψ,ξ)⟩𝒟​(𝒜∗)′,𝒟⁡(𝒜∗)=r⁡(b​ρs​ϕ⁡(2​π)¯+ρs​us​ψ⁡(2​π)¯−ξ⁡(2​π)¯).\left<{\mathcal{B}_{u}r(t)},{(\phi,\psi,\xi)}\right>_{\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})^{\prime},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})}=r\left(b\rho_{s}\overline{\phi(2\pi)}+\rho_{s}u_{s}\overline{\psi(2\pi)}-\overline{\xi(2\pi)}\right).

‖(ρ,u,S)‖C⁡([0,T];(L2​(0,2​π)3)CLOSE⩽C⁡(‖(ρ0,u0,S0)‖𝒵+‖r‖L2​(0,T)),\displaystyle\|(\rho,u,S)\|_{C([0,T];(L^{2}(0,2\pi)^{3})}\leqslant C\Big(\|(\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0})\|_{\mathcal{Z}}+\|r\|_{L^{2}(0,T)}\Big),

where C=C⁡(T)C=C(T) is a positive constant, independent of ρ0,u0,S0,r\rho_{0},u_{0},S_{0},r and tt.

5. Small time lack of controllability

5.1. Interior control

In this section, we study the lack of exact controllability of the system (1.4) when the localized interior control is acting on the density equation. Similar result holds true for the remaining two cases (control in velocity or control in stress). We establish the result by violating the observability inequality on an appropriate solution of the corresponding adjoint system. Our proof is in the same spirit of [3, Section 3]. We first find a candidate function as a terminal data of the transport equation and exploit the lack of controllability of the same in small time.

Without loss of generality, we consider the control domain 𝒪=(l1,l2),0⩽l1<l2<2​π.\mathcal{O}=(l_{1},l_{2}),0\leqslant l_{1}<l_{2}<2\pi.

Let us denote β=min⁡{|βi|,i=1,2,3}\beta=\min\{|\beta_{i}|,i=1,2,3\} and consider β​T<max⁡{l1,2​π−l2}\beta T<\max\{l_{1},2\pi-l_{2}\}. Then the system (1.4) is not exactly controllable in time TT by means of the controls fi∈L2(0,T;L2(𝒪)),i=1,2,3f_{i}\in L^{2}\left(0,T;L^{2}(\mathcal{O})\right),i=1,2,3 acting on every equations of (1.4).

satisfies that supp​(σ^)∩[0,T]×𝒪=∅\text{supp}(\hat{\sigma})\cap[0,T]\times\mathcal{O}=\emptyset (see also [3, Section 3]). Remark 5.2.

In Theorem 5.1, if the control domain 𝒪\mathcal{O} is (0,l2),(0,l_{2}), the we get the lack of controllability when T<2​π−l2β.T<\frac{2\pi-l_{2}}{\beta}. Similarly, one can prove the negative controllability result for the control domain 𝒪=(l1,2​π)\mathcal{O}=(l_{1},2\pi) at the time T<l1β.T<\frac{l_{1}}{\beta}.

5.2. Boundary control

Using the similar argument as done in the interior control case, here we will show that the system (1.8)-(1.10) is not controllable in small time by means of boundary control acting on the velocity. Other boundary control cases (1.8)-(1.9), (1.8)-(1.11) can be done similarly.

6. Rapid exponential stabilization

Let us recall the control system (1.8). The goal of this section is to study the boundary stabilization issues for (1.8) with single boundary control force. More precisely, we construct a stationary feedback law q⁡(t)q(t), r⁡(t)r(t) or p⁡(t)p(t) of the form Π⁡(ρ⁡(t,⋅),u⁡(t,⋅),S⁡(t,⋅))\Pi\left(\rho(t,\cdot),u(t,\cdot),S(t,\cdot)\right) such that the solution of the closed loop system (1.8) decays exponentially to zero at any prescribed decay rate. At first we describe Urquiza’s approach [38] which is the key argument of this section.

6.1. Urquiza’s method

Let us consider an abstract control system

(6.1) {y˙(t)=𝒜y(t)+ℬq(t),t∈(0,T),y⁡(0)=y0,\begin{cases}\dot{y}(t)=\mathcal{A}y(t)+\mathcal{B}q(t),\quad t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=y_{0},\end{cases}

where y⁡(t)∈ℋ,y0∈ℋ,q∈L2​(0,T)y(t)\in\mathcal{H},y_{0}\in\mathcal{H},q\in L^{2}(0,T), ℬ\mathcal{B} is an unbounded operator from ℂ\mathbb{C} to ℋ\mathcal{H}. 𝒜:D⁡(𝒜)⊂ℋ→ℋ\mathcal{A}:D(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H} is an unbounded operator and 𝒟⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}) is dense in ℋ.\mathcal{H}. To employ the method of Urquiza, one needs to take the following assumptions on the operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}:

  • (H1)

    𝒜\mathcal{A} is the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous group {et​𝒜}t∈ℝ\{e^{t\mathcal{A}}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}} on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

  • (H2)

    ℬ:ℂ→𝒟​(𝒜∗)′\mathcal{B}:\mathbb{C}\to\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})^{\prime} is linear and continuous.

  • (H3)

    Regularity property. For all T>0T>0 there exists C⁡(T)>0C(T)>0 such that

    ∫0T|ℬ∗​e−t​𝒜∗​yT|2⩽C​‖yT‖ℋ2,∀yT∈𝒟⁡(𝒜∗).\int_{0}^{T}\left|\mathcal{B}^{*}e^{-t\mathcal{A}^{*}}y_{T}\right|^{2}\leqslant C\left\|y_{T}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{H}},\quad\forall\,y_{T}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*}).
  • (H4)

    Controllability property. There are two constants T>0T>0 and c⁡(T)>0c(T)>0 such that

    ∫0T|ℬ∗​e−t​𝒜∗​yT|2≥c​‖yT‖ℋ2,∀yT∈𝒟⁡(𝒜∗).\int_{0}^{T}\left|\mathcal{B}^{*}e^{-t\mathcal{A}^{*}}y_{T}\right|^{2}\geq c\left\|y_{T}\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{H}},\quad\forall\,y_{T}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*}).

These hypotheses lead to the the following stabilization result. Its proof relies on algebraic Riccati equation associated with the linear quadratic regulator problem [19]. Let us introduce the growth bound of the semigroup {e𝒜​t}t≥0\{e^{\mathcal{A}t}\}_{t\geq 0} of continuous linear operator as follows:

g⁡(𝒜)=inft>01t​log⁡‖et​𝒜‖ℒ⁡(ℋ).g(\mathcal{A})=\inf_{t>0}\frac{1}{t}\log\left\|e^{t\mathcal{A}}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}.
Theorem 6.1.

[Urquiza [38], Theorem 2.12.1] Consider operators 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} under assumptions (H1)-(H4). For any ω>max⁡(g⁡(−𝒜),0)\omega>\max\left(g(-\mathcal{A}),0\right), we have

  • (i)

    The symmetric positive operator Λω\Lambda_{\omega} defined by

    ⟨Λω​x,z⟩ℋ=∫0∞⟨ℬ∗​e−τ​(𝒜+ω​I)∗​x,ℬ∗​e−τ​(𝒜+ω​I)∗​z⟩ℂ​𝑑τ,∀x,z∈ℋ\left<{\Lambda_{\omega}x},{z}\right>_{\mathcal{H}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left<{\mathcal{B}^{*}e^{-\tau(\mathcal{A}+\omega I)^{*}}x},{\mathcal{B}^{*}e^{-\tau(\mathcal{A}+\omega I)^{*}}z}\right>_{\mathbb{C}}d\tau,\,\forall\,x,z\in\mathcal{H}

    is coercive and is an isomorphism on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

  • (ii)

    Let Πω:=−ℬ∗​Λω−1\Pi_{\omega}:=-\mathcal{B}^{*}\Lambda_{\omega}^{-1}. The operator 𝒜+ℬ​Πω\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B}\Pi_{\omega} with 𝒟⁡(𝒜+ℬ​Πω)=Λω​(𝒟⁡(𝒜∗))\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B}\Pi_{\omega})=\Lambda_{\omega}(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*})) is the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous semigroup on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

  • (iii)

    The closed-loop system (6.1) with q=Πω​(y)q=\Pi_{\omega}(y) is exponentially stable that is,

    ‖et⁡(𝒜+ℬ​Πω)​x‖ℋ⩽C​e(−2​ω+g⁡(−𝒜))​t​‖x‖ℋ,∀x∈ℋ,\left\|e^{t(\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B}\Pi_{\omega})}x\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leqslant Ce^{\left(-2\omega+g(-\mathcal{A})\right)t}\left\|x\right\|_{\mathcal{H}},\forall x\in\mathcal{H},

    where CC is a positive constant.

We utilize Theorem 6.1 to prove the complete exponential stabilization of the linearized compressible Navier-Stokes equation with Maxwell’s law (1.8)-(1.9) with boundary feedback law.

6.2. Control in density

To apply the method mentioned above we need to show that all the assumptions (H1)-(H4) hold true for our system (4.1). Let us recall the corresponding spatial operator (𝒜,𝒟⁡(𝒜,𝒵m,m)CLOSE(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{Z}_{m,m}), where 𝒵m,m=L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)×L˙2​(0,2​π)\mathcal{Z}_{m,m}=\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi)\times\dot{L}^{2}(0,2\pi).

It can be check that the operator (𝒜,𝒟⁡(𝒜,𝒵m,m)CLOSE(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{Z}_{m,m}) generates a strongly continuous group {𝕋t}t∈ℝ\{\mathbb{T}_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}} of continuous linear operator. Hence (H1) holds. Also (H2) is true, see (4.3). We get (H3) and (H4) by Ingham inequality.

A similar process will give the complete stabilization for the control systems (1.8)-(1.10) and (1.8)-(1.11).

7. Construction of the biorthogonal family and Ingham-type inequality

This section is devoted to the proof of a suitable Ingham-type inequality which essentially helps to derive the required observability inequality. The proof of the Ingham-type inequality relies on the construction of a biorthogonal family of {e−λkl​t}k∈ℤ∗,l∈{1,2,3}\{e^{-{\lambda_{k}^{l}}t}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^{*},l\in\{1,2,3\}}. All the constants used in this section while finding the relevant estimates are generic, which may vary from line to line.

Let us assume ( H ). We recall the expressions of the eigenvalues of 𝒜\mathcal{A} in the following manner.

(7.1) λn1=−ω1+i​β1​n+O⁡(1|n|),n∈ℤ∗,λn2=−ω2+i​β2​n+O⁡(1|n|),n∈ℤ∗,λn3=−ω3+i​β3​n+O⁡(1|n|)n∈ℤ∗.}\left.\begin{aligned} \lambda_{n}^{1}=&-\omega_{1}+i\beta_{1}n+O\left(\frac{1}{|n|}\right),&n\in\mathbbm{Z}^{*},\\ \lambda_{n}^{2}=&-\omega_{2}+i\beta_{2}n+O\left(\frac{1}{|n|}\right),&n\in\mathbbm{Z}^{*},\\ \lambda_{n}^{3}=&-\omega_{3}+i\beta_{3}n+O\left(\frac{1}{|n|}\right)&n\in\mathbbm{Z}^{*}.\end{aligned}\right\}

We further denote the following notation:

Σ={(n,j):n∈ℤ∗,1⩽j⩽3}.\Sigma=\{(n,j):n\in\mathbb{Z}^{*},1\leqslant j\leqslant 3\}.
Lemma 7.1 (Gap properties of the spectrum).

For any (n,j),(k,l)∈Σ(n,j),(k,l)\in\Sigma, there exists C^>0\hat{C}>0 depending on ω1,ω2,ω3,β1,β2,β3\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\omega_{3},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}, such that

(7.2) |λnj−λkl|≥C^.\left|\lambda_{n}^{j}-\lambda_{k}^{l}\right|\geq\hat{C}.
Proof.

Note that ω1,ω2,ω3\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\omega_{3} are distinct and β1,β2,β3\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3} are also distinct. Thanks to the asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalues (7.1), we have a large N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that for (n,j),(k,j)∈Σ, with ​n≠k(n,j),(k,j)\in\Sigma,\text{ with }n\neq k and |n|,|k|>N|n|,|k|>N,

|λnj−λkj|≥|ℑ⁡(λnj−λkj)|≥C​|βj​(n−k)|≥C​|βj|.\left|\lambda_{n}^{j}-\lambda_{k}^{j}\right|\geq\left|\Im({\lambda_{n}^{j}-\lambda_{k}^{j}})\right|\geq C\left|\beta_{j}(n-k)\right|\geq C|\beta_{j}|.

Analogously, for (n,j),(k,l)∈Σ,j≠l(n,j),(k,l)\in\Sigma,j\neq l, |n|,|k|>N|n|,|k|>N, we have

|λnj−λkl|≥|ℜ⁡(λnj−λkl)|≥C​|ωj−ωl|.\left|\lambda_{n}^{j}-\lambda_{k}^{l}\right|\geq\left|\Re({\lambda_{n}^{j}-\lambda_{k}^{l}})\right|\geq C\left|\omega_{j}-\omega_{l}\right|.

As the eigenvalues are simple, we also find the gap condition (7.2) for finite number of the lower frequencies. ∎

Let us first define the exponential type and sine type functions.

Definition 7.2 (Entire functions of exponential type).

An entire function ff is said to be of exponential type AA if there exist positive constants A,BA,B such that

|f⁡(z)|⩽B​eA​|z|,z∈ℂ,\displaystyle|f(z)|\leqslant Be^{A|z|},\,z\in\mathbb{C},

and of exponential type at most AA, if for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exits Bϵ>0B_{\epsilon}>0 such that

|f⁡(z)|⩽Bϵ​e(A+ϵ)​|z|,z∈ℂ.\displaystyle|f(z)|\leqslant B_{\epsilon}\,e^{(A+\epsilon)|z|},\,z\in\mathbb{C}.
Definition 7.3.

(Sine type function) An entire function ff of exponential type π\pi is said to be of sine type if

  • •

    the zeros of f⁡(z)f(z), say μk\mu_{k} satisfy the gap condition, i.e., there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that |μk−μl|>δ|\mu_{k}-\mu_{l}|>\delta for k≠lk\neq l, and

  • •

    there exist positive constants C1C_{1},C2C_{2} and C3C_{3} such that

    C1​eπ​|y|⩽|f⁡(x+i​y)|⩽C2​eπ​|y|,∀x,y∈ℝ​ with |y|≥C3.C_{1}e^{\pi|y|}\leqslant|f(x+iy)|\leqslant C_{2}e^{\pi|y|},\,\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{R}\text{ with }|y|\geq C_{3}.

The following proposition states some important properties of sine-type functions (see Remark and Lemma 2, p.164 of [29] and Lemma 2, p.172 of [44] for details):

Proposition 7.4.

Let ff be a sine type function, and let {μk}k∈ℐ\{\mu_{k}\}_{k\in\mathcal{I}} with ℐ⊂ℤ\mathcal{I}\subset\mathbb{Z} be its sequence of zeros. Then, we have:

  • •

    for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exist constants Kϵ,K~ϵ>0K_{\epsilon},\tilde{K}_{\epsilon}>0 such that

    Kϵ​eπ​|y|⩽|f⁡(x+i​y)|⩽K~ϵ​eπ​|y|, if dist(x+i​y,{μk})>ϵ,K_{\epsilon}e^{\pi|y|}\leqslant|f(x+iy)|\leqslant\tilde{K}_{\epsilon}e^{\pi|y|},\text{ if dist$\left(x+iy,\{\mu_{k}\}\right)>\epsilon$},
  • •

    there exist some constants K1,K2>0K_{1},K_{2}>0 such that

    K1<|f′​(μk)|<K2,∀k∈ℐ.K_{1}<|f^{\prime}(\mu_{k})|<K_{2},\quad\forall k\in\mathcal{I}.

The main goal of this section is to find a class of entire functions 𝒢={Ψkj}(k,j)∈Σ\mathcal{G}=\{\Psi_{k}^{j}\}_{(k,j)\in\Sigma} with the following properties:

  • 1.

    The family 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains entire functions of exponential type T2\frac{T}{2}. That means there exists a positive constant CC such that

    (7.3) |Ψkj​(z)|⩽C​eT2​|z|,∀z∈ℂ,(k,j)∈Σ.\displaystyle\left|\Psi_{k}^{j}(z)\right|\leqslant Ce^{\frac{T}{2}\left|z\right|},\quad\forall z\in\mathbb{C},\,\,(k,j)\in\Sigma.
  • 2.

    All the members of 𝒢\mathcal{G} are square-integrable on the real line, i.e.,

    (7.4) ∫ℝ|Ψkj​(x)|2​𝑑x<∞.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\Psi_{k}^{j}(x)\right|^{2}\,{\rm d}x<\infty.

Let us now state the celebrated Paley-Wiener theorem, from which we can conclude about the desired biorthogonal family using the family 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Theorem 7.5 (Paley-Wiener).

[44, Theorem 1.8] Let ff be an entire function of exponential type AA and suppose

∫−∞∞|f⁡(x)|2​𝑑x<∞.\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f(x)|^{2}\,{\rm d}x<\infty.

Then there exists a function ϕ∈L2​(−A,A)\phi\in L^{2}(-A,A) with the following representation

f⁡(z)=∫−AAei​z​t​ϕ​(t)​𝑑t,z∈ℂ.\displaystyle f(z)=\int_{-A}^{A}e^{izt}\phi(t)\,{\rm d}t,\,z\in\mathbb{C}.

Thus if we have the existence of such family 𝒢\mathcal{G} of entire functions satisfying (7.3)-(7.4), then applying the Paley-Wiener theorem for the same, one can get a family of functions 𝒥={Θkj,}(k,j)∈Σ\mathcal{J}=\{\Theta_{k}^{j},\}_{(k,j)\in\Sigma} supported in [−T2,T2][-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}], such that the following representation holds

(7.5) Ψkj​(z)=∫−T2T2ei​z​t​Θkj​(t)​𝑑t,z∈ℂ.\displaystyle\Psi_{k}^{j}(z)=\int_{-\frac{T}{2}}^{\frac{T}{2}}e^{izt}\Theta_{k}^{j}(t)dt,\,z\in\mathbb{C}.

Clearly, Θkj\Theta_{k}^{j} are the Fourier transformations of Ψkj\Psi_{k}^{j} respectively, for (k,j)∈Σ.(k,j)\in\Sigma. Also, by Plancharel’s Theorem, we have

∫ℝ|Ψkj​(x)|2=2​π​∫−T2T2|Θkj​(t)|2​𝑑t.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\Psi_{k}^{j}(x)\right|^{2}=2\pi\int_{-\frac{T}{2}}^{\frac{T}{2}}\left|\Theta_{k}^{j}(t)\right|^{2}\,{\rm d}t.

Let PP be the canonical product defined in (7.6). Then PP is an entire function of exponential type π⁡(1|β1|+1|β2|+1|β3|)\pi\left(\frac{1}{|\beta_{1}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{2}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{3}|}\right), which satisfies the following properties:

Theorem 7.8.

Let T>2​π​(1|β1|+1|β2|+1|β3|).T>2\pi\left(\frac{1}{|\beta_{1}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{2}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{3}|}\right). Then there exists a family {Θnj}(n,j)∈Σ\{\Theta_{n}^{j}\}_{(n,j)\in\Sigma} which is biorthogonal to the family of exponentials {e−λkl​t}(k,l)∈Σ\{e^{-{\lambda_{k}^{l}}t}\}_{(k,l)\in\Sigma} in L2​(−T2,T2)L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right), i.e.,

(7.18) ∫−T2T2Θnj​(t)​e−λkl¯​t​𝑑t=δn​k​δj​l.\int_{-\frac{T}{2}}^{\frac{T}{2}}\Theta_{n}^{j}(t)e^{-\overline{\lambda_{k}^{l}}t}\,{\rm d}t=\delta_{nk}\delta_{jl}.

Moreover, there exists a positive constant C>0C>0 such that the following estimate holds:

(7.19) ‖∑(n,j)∈Σanj​Θnj‖L2​(−T2,T2)2⩽C​∑(n,j)∈Σ|anj|2,\left\|\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}a_{n}^{j}\Theta_{n}^{j}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right)}^{2}\leqslant C\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}|a_{n}^{j}|^{2},

Proof.

Ψnj​(z):=P⁡(z)(z−i​λnj¯)​P′​(i​λnj¯).\Psi_{n}^{j}(z):=\frac{P(z)}{(z-i\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}})P^{\prime}\left(i\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}}\right)}.

2​π​∫−T′2T′2|Θkj​(t)|2​𝑑t=∫ℝ|Ψkj​(x)|2​𝑑x⩽C.2\pi\int_{-\frac{T^{\prime}}{2}}^{\frac{T^{\prime}}{2}}\left|\Theta_{k}^{j}(t)\right|^{2}\,{\rm d}t=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left|\Psi_{k}^{j}(x)\right|^{2}\,{\rm d}x\leqslant C.

The following corollary is an immediate consequence of the above theorem which will essentially give us the required Ingham-type inequality.

Corollary 7.9.

Let us assume T>2​π​(1|β1|+1|β2|+1|β3|).T>2\pi\left(\frac{1}{|\beta_{1}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{2}|}+\frac{1}{|\beta_{3}|}\right). Then for any finite sequence of scalars {anj}(n,j)∈Σ\{a_{n}^{j}\}_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}, there exist two positive constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} such that the following inequality holds:

(7.22) C1​∑(n,j)∈Σ|anj|2⩽‖∑(n,j)∈Σanj​e−λnj¯​t‖L2​(−T2,T2)2⩽C2​∑(n,j)∈Σ|anj|2.C_{1}\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}|a_{n}^{j}|^{2}\leqslant\left\|\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}a_{n}^{j}e^{-\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}}t}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right)}^{2}\leqslant C_{2}\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}|a_{n}^{j}|^{2}.
Proof.

Using (7.18), we can deduce

∑(n,j)∈Σ|anj|2=\displaystyle\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}|a_{n}^{j}|^{2}= ∫−T2T2(∑(n,j)∈Σanj​e−λnj¯​t)​(∑(k,l)∈Σakl¯​Θkl​(t))​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{T}{2}}^{\frac{T}{2}}{\left(\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}a_{n}^{j}e^{-\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}}t}\right)}\left(\sum_{(k,l)\in\Sigma}\overline{a_{k}^{l}}\Theta_{k}^{l}(t)\right)\,{\rm d}t
(7.23) ⩽\displaystyle\leqslant ‖∑(n,j)∈Σanj​e−λnj¯​t‖L2​(−T2,T2)​‖∑(n,j)∈Σakl¯​Θkl‖L2​(−T2,T2).\displaystyle\left\|\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}a_{n}^{j}e^{-\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}}t}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right)}\left\|\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}\overline{a_{k}^{l}}\Theta_{k}^{l}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right)}.

The inequality (7.23) along with (7.19) establish the left inequality of (7.22).

Straightforward estimate provides the right hand inequality. Indeed,

‖∑(n,j)∈Σanj​e−λnj¯​t‖L2​(−T2,T2)2⩽C2​∑j=13‖∑n∈ℤ∗anj​e−λnj¯​t‖L2​(−T2,T2)2.\displaystyle\left\|\sum_{(n,j)\in\Sigma}a_{n}^{j}e^{-\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}}t}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right)}^{2}\leqslant C_{2}\sum_{j=1}^{3}\left\|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{*}}a_{n}^{j}e^{-\overline{\lambda_{n}^{j}}t}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(-\frac{T}{2},\frac{T}{2}\right)}^{2}.

Next, utilizing the Ingham-type inequality [1, Proposition 8.1], one can get the right hand inequality.∎

8. Some details on multiple eigenvalues

Recall from Remark 2.7 that 𝒜\mathcal{A} can have multiple eigenvalues. In this section, we will demonstrate that results analogous to Lemma 2.8 and Proposition 2.10 also apply in this context. This will enable us to extend our analysis to prove Theorem 1.2, Theorem 1.5, and Theorem 1.8. We will specifically focus on the case where 𝒜\mathcal{A} has double eigenvalues. Using a similar approach, we can also handle the case when 𝒜\mathcal{A} has triple eigenvalues.

Proposition 8.1.

For each n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, let us denote

(8.1) qn​(λ)=−b+(λ+i​n​us)2ρs​n2−μ​κ​(λ+i​n​us)2ρs2​(1+κ​λ)2.q_{n}(\lambda)=-b+\frac{\left({\lambda}+inu_{s}\right)^{2}}{\rho_{s}n^{2}}-\frac{\mu\kappa\left({\lambda}+inu_{s}\right)^{2}}{\rho_{s}^{2}\left(1+\kappa{\lambda}\right)^{2}}.

Then λ\lambda is a double root of the characteristic equation (2.13) if and only if qn​(λ)=0q_{n}(\lambda)=0.

From the relation between roots and coefficients in (2.15)-(2.20), the above result follows by a direct calculation.

Let for some n∈ℤ∗n\in\mathbb{Z}^{*}, 𝒜\mathcal{A} has eigenvalues λn1,λn2,λn3\lambda_{n}^{1},\lambda_{n}^{2},\lambda_{n}^{3} with λn2=λn3​(suppose ​λn2​ is a double eigenvalue)\lambda_{n}^{2}=\lambda_{n}^{3}\left(\text{suppose }\lambda_{n}^{2}\text{ is a double eigenvalue}\right). Proposition 8.1 gives that qn​(λn2)=0q_{n}(\lambda_{n}^{2})=0.

ξn,1=1θn,1​(−1λn1+i​n​usi​n​ρsμ⁡(λn1+i​n​us)ρs​(1+κ​λn1))​ei​n​x,ξn,2=1θn,2​(−1λn2+i​n​usi​n​ρsμ⁡(λn2+i​n​us)ρs​(1+κ​λn2))​ei​n​x,\displaystyle\xi_{n,1}=\frac{1}{\theta_{n,1}}\begin{pmatrix}-1\vskip 2.84526pt\\ \frac{\lambda_{n}^{1}+inu_{s}}{{in\rho_{s}}}\vskip 2.84526pt\\ \frac{\mu\left(\lambda_{n}^{1}+inu_{s}\right)}{\rho_{s}\left(1+\kappa\lambda_{n}^{1}\right)}\end{pmatrix}e^{inx},\quad\xi_{n,2}=\frac{1}{\theta_{n,2}}\begin{pmatrix}-1\vskip 2.84526pt\\ \frac{\lambda_{n}^{2}+inu_{s}}{{in\rho_{s}}}\vskip 2.84526pt\\ \frac{\mu\left(\lambda_{n}^{2}+inu_{s}\right)}{\rho_{s}\left(1+\kappa\lambda_{n}^{2}\right)}\end{pmatrix}e^{inx},
ξn,3=1θn,2​(cn−1+cn​(λn2+i​n​us)i​n​ρsμ​κ​(λn2+i​n​us)−μ⁡(1+κ​λn2)​(1+cn​(λn2+i​n​us))ρs​(1+κ​λn2)2)​ei​n​x,\displaystyle\xi_{n,3}=\frac{1}{\theta_{n,2}}\begin{pmatrix}c_{n}\vskip 2.84526pt\\ -\frac{1+c_{n}\left(\lambda_{n}^{2}+inu_{s}\right)}{in\rho_{s}}\vskip 2.84526pt\\ \frac{\mu\kappa\left(\lambda_{n}^{2}+inu_{s}\right)-\mu\left(1+\kappa\lambda_{n}^{2}\right)\left(1+c_{n}\left(\lambda_{n}^{2}+inu_{s}\right)\right)}{\rho_{s}\left(1+\kappa\lambda_{n}^{2}\right)^{2}}\end{pmatrix}e^{inx},

The families {ξn,l| 1⩽l⩽3,n∈ℕ}\left\{\xi_{n,l}\>|\>1\leqslant l\leqslant 3,n\in\mathbb{N}\right\} and {ξn,l∗| 1⩽l⩽3,n∈ℕ}\left\{\xi^{*}_{n,l}\>|\>1\leqslant l\leqslant 3,n\in\mathbb{N}\right\} satisfy the bi-orthonormality relations (2.46) and Proposition 2.10 holds.

Since in the case of double eigenvalues of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we obtain the result analogous to Proposition 2.10 using the generalized eigenvectors of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*}, the proof of the null controllability result can be adapted to the case when 𝒜\mathcal{A} has double eigenvalues. The essential modifications of the proof of the controllability results to this case are indicated below.

Remark 8.2.

𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} in Lemma 2.12 and ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} in Lemma 2.13 are given by

(8.5) 𝒜n=(λn1000λn2−100λn2),ℬn=b​2​π​(1ψ¯n,11λn2​ψ¯n,21ψ¯n,2).\mathcal{A}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{n}^{1}&0&0\\ 0&\lambda_{n}^{2}&-1\\ 0&0&\lambda_{n}^{2}\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathcal{B}_{n}=b\sqrt{2\pi}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{{\bar{\psi}_{n,1}}}\\ \frac{1}{{\lambda_{n}^{2}\bar{\psi}_{n,2}}}\\ \frac{1}{{\bar{\psi}_{n,2}}}\end{pmatrix}.

We can see that,

Rank[λI−𝒜n;ℬn]=3, for λ=λn1,λn2,λn3.\displaystyle\text{Rank}\left[\lambda I-\mathcal{A}_{n}\;;\;\mathcal{B}_{n}\right]=3,\>\text{ for }\lambda=\lambda^{1}_{n},\lambda^{2}_{n},\lambda^{3}_{n}.

Thus the finite dimensional system (2.76) is controllable.

The rest of the proof of Theorem 1.5 in the case of multiple eigenvalues is same as given in Section 3.

In the case of double eigenvalues, to complete the proofs of Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.8, we need to adjust the finitely many modes in the Ingham inequality where the double eigenvalues exist. For this adjustment, it is essential that the eigenfunction ξn,l∗\xi^{*}_{n,l}, where l=1,2,3l=1,2,3, satisfies the unique continuation property. In the following, we will verify this property for the case of density control. Using a similar approach, we can also prove the unique continuation property when the control acts only on the velocity or stress.

Interior controllability. Control in density: Here the observation operator ℬ∗∈ℒ⁡(𝒵m,L2​(0,2​π))\mathcal{B}^{*}\in\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{Z}_{m},L^{2}\left(0,2\pi\right)\right) is given by

(8.6) ℬ∗​(ϕ1ϕ2ϕ3)=b​𝟙𝒪1​ϕ1.\mathcal{B}^{*}\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{1}\\ \phi_{2}\\ \phi_{3}\end{pmatrix}=b\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{O}_{1}}\phi_{1}.

From (8.6), (8.2), (8.3), (8.4), and (2.45), it is clear that ℬ∗​(ξn,l∗)≠0\mathcal{B}^{*}\left(\xi^{*}_{n,l}\right)\neq 0, for l=1,2,3l=1,2,3.

Boundary controllability. Control in density: Here the observation operator ℬ∗∈ℒ⁡(𝒟⁡(𝒜∗),ℂ)\mathcal{B}^{*}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}^{*});\mathbb{C}) is given by

(8.7) ℬ∗​(ϕ,ψ,ξ)=b​us​ϕ​(2​π)+b​ρs​ψ​(2​π).\mathcal{B}^{*}(\phi,\psi,\xi)=bu_{s}{\phi(2\pi)}+b\rho_{s}{\psi(2\pi)}.

From (8.7), (8.2), (8.3), (8.4), and (2.45), it is clear that ℬ∗​(ξn,l∗)≠0\mathcal{B}^{*}\left(\xi^{*}_{n,l}\right)\neq 0, for l=1,2,3l=1,2,3.
